summary: This document specifies a general channel mechanism, as extensions to TRILL, for sending messages such as BFD between RBridges and between RBridges and end stations in an RBridge campus.

eli5.summary: This builds a private side-lane inside a network so switches can send each other their own control notes.

questions: what is the rbridge channel ethertype
how does trill carry bfd messages
subtitle: A general side channel that lets TRILL switches send each other control messages such as BFD.

tldr.problem: The TRILL base protocol only carries TRILL Data messages and TRILL IS-IS messages, so there is no standard way for RBridges to exchange other messages such as BFD continuity checks.
tldr.mechanism: RBridge Channel messages are dressed up as TRILL Data frames with a special inner destination address (All-Egress-RBridges) and the RBridge-Channel Ethertype, followed by a small channel header that names the protocol being carried.
tldr.outcome: Any protocol can reuse one channel format for single-hop, multi-hop and multi-destination delivery, including a native form for talking to directly connected end stations. RFC 7978 later updated this document.

today: RFC 7178 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014 and has been updated by RFC 7978. It is not marked as obsoleted.

sections.title: Why TRILL Needs a Channel
sections.content:
TRILL switches, called RBridges, forward traffic using IS-IS routing. The base protocol in RFC 6325 provides only for TRILL Data messages and TRILL IS-IS messages. This document adds a general RBridge Channel for sending other messages, such as BFD messages (RFC 5880), between RBridges and between RBridges and end stations on the same link.

The motivation is that many protocols are expected to run at the TRILL layer, for example rapid continuity checking with BFD. Rather than design a carriage method for each one, the channel supports single-hop and multi-hop unicast as well as VLAN-scoped multi-destination distribution. It is also designed to work with minimal configuration.

The RFC compares the idea to the MPLS Generic Associated Channel (RFC 5586). The difference is that MPLS uses a special label, while an RBridge Channel message is flagged by a special multicast inner destination address and inner Ethertype.
sections.eli5: Switches only had two kinds of mail: passenger traffic and routing news. This adds a third mailbox for any other kind of note they want to send each other.

sections.title: The Channel Message Format
sections.content:
Between RBridges, a channel message travels as a TRILL Data frame. It is recognized by its Inner.MacDA, which is the All-Egress-RBridges multicast address, together with the inner Ethertype, the RBridge-Channel Ethertype. The frame is built from a link header, a TRILL header, an inner Ethernet header, the RBridge Channel header, a protocol-specific payload and a link trailer.

The RBridge Channel header begins with the Ethertype and then a four-byte quantity with four sub-fields: CHV (4 bits, the header version, which is zero in this document), Channel Protocol (12 bits), Flags (12 bits) and ERR (4 bits, used for error reporting).

Three flag bits are defined: SL (Silent, suppresses error messages), MH (Multi-Hop, says whether the message may be multi-hop) and NA (Native, see below). The remaining flag bits are reserved, MUST be sent as zero and are ignored on receipt. The only protocol value defined here is 0x001, the RBridge Channel Error protocol.

The originating RBridge sets the inner source MAC address (Inner.MacSA) to a MAC address unique within the campus that it owns, in effect the address of a virtual internal end station.
sections.eli5: Each note has an envelope with a stamp saying 'this is a channel note', then a small label giving the note type, a few tick boxes, and room for an error code.

sections.title: TRILL Header, VLAN and Priority
sections.content:
The TRILL header follows the base rules: the version is zero, the M bit says whether the frame is known unicast (M=0) or multi-destination (M=1), and a new channel message starts with the Hop Count at its maximum, 0x3F, unless a channel protocol specifies otherwise. For messages sent a known number of hops, using the maximum and checking it on receipt gives an extra validity check.

The Ingress Nickname is one held by the originating RBridge. The Egress Nickname depends on the case: for multi-destination messages it designates the distribution tree, for multi-hop unicast it is the target RBridge's nickname, and for one-hop unicast it is either the neighbor's nickname or the special Any-RBridge nickname. RBridges supporting the channel MUST accept frames carrying Any-RBridge as addressed to them, which guarantees processing by an immediate neighbor whatever the state of nicknames.

An inner VLAN tag is always present. Multi-destination messages are VLAN scoped, so the VLAN ID MUST be set to the VLAN of interest, while known unicast messages default to VLAN 1. For priority, the RFC recommends 7 for one-hop messages critical to connectivity (such as one-hop BFD), 6 for other important unicast messages, and the default of zero for the rest, with priorities above 5 not to be used for those.
sections.eli5: The envelope has a from and to name. A special 'anyone next door' name lets a switch reach its neighbor even if nobody has been given a name yet. Urgent notes get a bigger priority sticker.

sections.title: Processing and Errors
sections.content:
A receiving RBridge treats a channel message like a regular TRILL Data frame, with three exceptions. It MUST recognize the Any-RBridge egress nickname, it MUST process the message even when it is not the egress if an RBridge Channel Alert extended header flag (from RFC 7179) is set, and on decapsulation it MUST check the Ethertype when the inner destination is All-Egress-RBridges.

The frame is discarded, and an error may be generated, if the Ethertype is unknown or truncated, the CHV is non-zero, the Channel Protocol is reserved or unknown, the ERR field is non-zero for a protocol other than 0x001, or the NA flag is set on a frame that should have arrived natively.

An RBridge Channel Error frame is a multi-hop unicast channel message sent back to the original ingress. It carries at least the first 256 bytes of the erroneous message. No error is sent if the Silent flag is set, if the problem was found only because of the Non-critical Channel Alert flag, if the bad frame is itself an error frame, or if rate limiting suppresses it. An RBridge MUST NOT answer an error message with another error message.

Errors inside a recognized channel protocol are handled by that protocol and do not produce RBridge Channel Error frames.
sections.eli5: If a switch gets a note it cannot read, it sends back a short 'I could not read this' reply with a piece of the note. It never replies to a reply like that, so they cannot get stuck in an endless loop.

sections.title: Error Codes
sections.content:
The ERR field in an error frame holds one of the codes below. Error frames should have the SL and MH flags set to one, the NA flag MUST be zero (or one for native frames) and ERR MUST be non-zero.

  • 1: frame too short (truncated Ethertype or channel header)
  • 2: unrecognized Ethertype
  • 3: unimplemented value of CHV
  • 4: wrong value of the NA flag
  • 5: channel protocol reserved or unimplemented

Values 6 to 14 are unassigned and 15 is reserved for a possible future error-code expansion feature.
sections.eli5: The reply has a number that says what went wrong: too short, strange stamp, wrong version, wrong delivery method, or unknown note type.

sections.title: Native Frames for End Stations
sections.content:
Some channel protocols need to talk to end stations directly connected to an RBridge. Native RBridge Channel frames do this on an Ethernet link. They look like the inner frame of a normal channel message, with these differences: a VLAN tag is not required by TRILL, the NA flag MUST be one, and the destination is either the unicast address of the target port or one of two multicast addresses.

  • An end station multicasting to all RBridges on a link that support the channel protocol uses All-Edge-RBridges.
  • An RBridge multicasting to the end stations on a link uses TRILL-End-Stations.

The protocol number space is shared with TRILL Data formatted messages. An RBridge may translate between the two forms if the channel protocol provides for it, and must at least flip the NA flag and fix the MAC addresses when doing so. Native error messages start the quoted part of the bad frame at the channel header, since there is no TRILL header, and are sent to the source MAC of the bad frame.
sections.eli5: Normally the notes stay between switches. The native form is a version of the note that a switch can hand to a computer plugged straight into it, and the computer can hand one back.

sections.title: Advertising Support and Congestion
sections.content:
Support for channel protocols is advertised through TLVs or sub-TLVs in an RBridge's Link State PDU as documented in RFC 7176. Protocols 0 and 0xFFF are reserved, and protocol 1 (the error protocol) MUST be implemented by any RBridge with the channel feature. Messages SHOULD only be sent to RBridges that advertise the protocol involved.

Channel traffic should stay small compared with link bandwidth. Outgoing messages SHOULD be rate limited so that aggressive connectivity checking does not cause congestion or become a denial-of-service attack. Connectivity-checking applications such as BFD SHOULD be limited to below 5% of the bitrate of the links involved. Incoming messages MAY be rate limited, honoring priority and drop eligibility.

Single-hop messages may, if the channel protocol allows, be sent over a link that is not yet fully up, in the Detect or 2-Way state as well as Report (RFC 7177).
sections.eli5: Control notes should be tiny compared to all the other traffic. If a switch sends too many it clogs the hallway, so switches should limit how many they send.

sections.title: Allocations and Security
sections.content:
IANA allocated the Any-RBridge nickname 0xFFC0 and two multicast addresses, 01-80-C2-00-00-45 (TRILL-End-Stations) and 01-80-C2-00-00-46 (All-Edge-RBridges). It also created registries for channel protocols, header flags and error codes. Protocols 0xFF8 to 0xFFE are reserved for Private Use and must be used only inside a private network. The IEEE Registration Authority assigned the Ethertype 0x8946 to TRILL RBridge Channel.

The channel provides no general integrity, authentication or encryption. A channel protocol that needs these MUST supply them itself, as the BFD authentication mechanism does. TRILL does not protect against forging of the Ingress Nickname or, in native frames, the outer source MAC address, which can misdirect responses or errors. Wrongly advertised support could send channel messages to an RBridge that does not handle them, but the RFC judges that unlikely to cause much harm because end stations will drop or refuse such frames.
sections.eli5: The notes have no lock on them, so any protocol that needs secrecy has to bring its own lock. A faked return address could send replies to the wrong place.
